question: What let the 2026-11-11 incident happen, and how do proven systems prevent each part of it?
found: Measured: after the reboot the agent replayed the afternoon's jobs from the oldest (102 started, 40 ok, 62 failed - mostly guards refusing), fifty at a time after a reconnect, on shared clones; it had inferred 'pending' from a missing result. Before that it stalled at 22:29 CET with nothing logged until the reboot. No alert could reach the author - every channel went through the agent. Harm: none - four replayed pull requests, all the legitimate tad 0.4.0 pin bump; no direct pushes, tags, releases or phone actions; tools and clones restored. The root: a job is a script with no record of its life. Proven answers: durable execution's event history and heartbeats (Temporal), leases with fencing tokens (Kleppmann; Patterns of Distributed Systems), a dead man's switch watched from elsewhere (Healthchecks), crash-only recovery (Candea and Fox), run-once jobs with deadlines (Kubernetes), idempotency keys (Stripe), a working tree per job (git worktree).

question: How should waiting be counted, and how can work go on while a long job runs?
found: Waiting is one of the seven wastes of the Toyota Production System; Kanban measures flow efficiency - time worked over total time - so manual work (effort) and waiting (idle time) are two halves of one measure. Little's law: shorter waits or more work in flight raise throughput. Make and CI run independent jobs side by side and serialise only those sharing a resource. So: lab-agent records every wait itself, with what is waited on and for which project; and jobs declare the resources they hold, so those that do not conflict run in parallel.
